doc.title: Jason Marsalis — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Listening without scores, NOCCA theory and the suggestion to try mallets
summary: He listened to classical records by ear while studying theory with Dr. Steven Danker at NOCCA. His father got him a set of vibes.

venues.name: New Orleans Center for Creative Arts

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Did you go consulting the scores? Or are you just taking in everything aurally?

No. I didn’t have any scores. I just put – I took the jazz musician [?] – I just put it on and would listen. I just listened to what instrument is doing what. What is going on? There was a lot of details that I found later, looking into the scores that I didn’t know

at the time, that amazed me even more. But I didn’t have – I didn’t use that. It’s great to do that, but at the time, I just didn’t do that. I just put it on and listened. Man, what is going on? It just amazed me. So that’s when I started to get into – at the time, I’m also attending the New Orleans Center for Creative Arts. There was a teacher, Dr. Steven Danker, who taught music theory and taught classical music in the repertoire. I was starting to get into that while listening to this. So I’m getting reinforced from education on a whole bunch of angles. While this is going on – and I just want to make this a real quick side note, because I thinking about it – at some point my father has this conversation with me. He says, “I see that you’re into percussion. I think it would be a good idea if you explored mallets.” I said, “Yeah, I think you might be right.” So he was able to get me a set of vibes. I started practicing on it, but at the time, my practicing was very inconsistent. It was, I practiced a little bit, then not as much, a little bit, not as much.
